conclusion: For the recorded large Benchy on the measured 16-core Windows host, the latest support-corrected baseline takes 43.542s median over three trials; a local contact-collision reuse candidate takes 42.654s with strongly overlapping ranges, so the experiment does not establish a stable substantial total speedup or halving. Sampled CPU medians fall from 300.641 to 292.516s and initial sampling medians from 7.092 to 5.008s. All 811657 ordered printer commands, motion role/width/height annotations and emitted configuration remain identical. Initial sampling mostly spends its worker elapsed time in roof and regular component geometry/line generation. Keep reuse local to a fixed batch/layer; changing a value-returning contact arm into a separate branch also prevents copies of ordinary reference-returning avoidance polygons. Further speed work needs complete-key geometry/fill reuse and profiling of support assembly, toolpaths and non-support stages, without changing deterministic publication or contact rules.

verification.summary: Preserved the committed support roof, belt grid, deterministic publication and inclined-landing behavior while reusing one local collision polygon per batch/layer and avoiding ordinary polygon copies. All three candidate slices match the latest baseline in all 811657 commands, motion annotations and emitted configuration; no failed branch warnings. The unchanged affected native tests passed 84 cases and 18107 assertions. Three-trial medians of 43.542s and 42.654s have overlapping ranges; this is not proof of a stable large total speedup or halving. Durable evidence is in docs/evidence/benchy-slicing-performance-20261016.md. File hashes bind reviewed bytes; commit fields are checkout anchors, not claims of committed changed source.
